name: Battle of Tarawa
info: United States Marines landed on Betio, the main island of Tarawa Atoll in the Gilbert Islands, on 20 November 1943 and took it from its Japanese garrison in 76 hours at a cost of nearly 6,400 lives on all sides.

facts.date: 20–23 November 1943; the landing was at 09:10 on 20 November and Betio was declared secure at 13:30 on 23 November
facts.place: Betio, the largest island of Tarawa Atoll in the Gilbert Islands, now part of the Republic of Kiribati but then a Japanese-occupied British colony
facts.sides: The United States, under Admiral Raymond Spruance, Admiral Richmond Kelly Turner and Major General Julian C. Smith, with the 2nd Marine Division (roughly 12,000 Marines on Tarawa); Japan, under Rear Admiral Keiji Shibazaki, with a garrison counted at 3,636 or at 4,500 defenders, besides about 1,200 Korean labourers
facts.outcome: American victory: Betio was taken and almost the whole garrison killed, with 4,690 of the island's defenders dead and 3,166 casualties in the 2nd Marine Division.

t: The battle was the first American offensive in the Central Pacific and the first time in the Pacific War that a United States amphibious landing met serious, well prepared Japanese opposition.

A neap tide left only about 3 feet of water over the reef, so most landing craft could not cross it and the Marines had to wade ashore or be carried in by tracked LVTs, half of which were knocked out on the first day.
Of the 3,636 Japanese in the garrison, only one officer and sixteen enlisted men survived, and only 129 of the 1,200 Korean labourers.
dyk: Marine cameramen filmed the dead on the beaches at Tarawa, and the decision on whether to release the footage was deferred to President Franklin D. Roosevelt, who approved it.
ev: Colonel Evans Carlson's raid on Makin Island makes the Japanese command aware of the vulnerability of the Gilbert Islands
The 6th Yokosuka Special Naval Landing Force reinforces Betio under Rear Admiral Tomonari
The Joint Chiefs of Staff direct Admiral Nimitz to plan an offensive in the Gilberts, and Rear Admiral Shibazaki relieves Tomonari
Marines land on the north shore of Betio under fire, with the tide too low for most landing craft to cross the reef
A Japanese counterattack at night and in the early hours is broken up, and Betio is declared secure on 23 November
A New York Times editorial warns that future assaults may cost even more, after public protest at the losses
The 2nd Marine Division is withdrawn, and Nimitz launches the Marshalls campaign ten weeks after Tarawa

sections.background:
The United States planned to take the Mariana Islands to set up forward air bases that could support operations across the Central Pacific, to the Philippines and towards Japan. Naval doctrine of the time held that land-based aircraft were needed to weaken defences and protect an invasion force. The nearest islands able to support such an effort against the Marianas were the Marshalls, but a Japanese garrison and air base on the island of Betio, in Tarawa Atoll in the Gilbert Islands, cut the Marshalls off from direct communications with Hawaii. American strategists therefore believed that the garrison and airfield on Tarawa would have to be neutralised first.

After the Guadalcanal campaign the 2nd Marine Division had been withdrawn to New Zealand, where its losses were replaced and its men recovered from malaria and other illnesses. On 20 July 1943 the Joint Chiefs of Staff directed Admiral Chester W. Nimitz to prepare plans for an offensive in the Gilbert Islands. In August Admiral Raymond A. Spruance flew to New Zealand to meet the division's new commander, General Julian C. Smith, and begin planning the invasion with his commanders.

Colonel Evans Carlson's diversionary raid on Makin Island in August 1942 had made the Japanese command aware of the vulnerability and strategic significance of the Gilberts. The 6th Yokosuka Special Naval Landing Force reinforced Betio in February 1943, and the Japanese then worked for nearly a year to fortify the island.
sections.forces:
Betio lies about 2,400 miles (3,900 km) south-west of Pearl Harbor, at the southern end of the lagoon. It is a small, flat island about 2 miles (3.2 km) long and at most 800 yards (730 m) wide, with a reef about 500 metres wide around it and a long pier on the north shore. The garrison belonged to the Imperial Japanese Navy. The 3rd Special Base Defense Force had 1,112 men and the 7th Sasebo Special Naval Landing Force, under Commander Takeo Sugai, 1,497, with 14 Type 95 light tanks. The 1,247 men of the 111th Pioneers and 970 of the Fourth Fleet's construction battalion had been brought in to build the defences, and about 1,200 of these men were Korean labourers.

Rear Admiral Tomonari Saichiro, an engineer, designed the defences, which were meant to stop the attackers in the water or pin them on the beaches. Rear Admiral Keiji Shibazaki replaced him on 20 July 1943 and is quoted as saying that it would take one million men one hundred years to conquer Tarawa. There were 14 coastal defence guns, among them four 8-inch Vickers guns, about 500 pillboxes, forty artillery pieces and trenches linking every point. The command expected any attack to come from the open western or southern waters, since the guns were thought to make entry to the lagoon very difficult.

The American force was the largest yet assembled for a single operation in the Pacific: 17 aircraft carriers, 12 battleships, 8 heavy cruisers, 4 light cruisers, 66 destroyers and 36 transports, carrying the 2nd Marine Division and the Army's 27th Infantry Division, about 35,000 troops in all. The 2nd Marine Division, under Julian C. Smith, was to take Betio.
sections.course:
Before dawn on 20 November the island's 8-inch guns opened fire on the invasion fleet, and the battleships Colorado and Maryland replied. Three of the four guns were knocked out quickly, which left the approach to the lagoon open. After an air attack at 06:10 the naval bombardment continued for three hours. Planners had expected 5 feet (1.5 m) of water over the reef, but a neap tide left a mean depth of 3 feet (0.9 m). Major Frank Holland, a New Zealand liaison officer, had warned of at most 3 feet.

The attack began at 09:00, thirty minutes late. Only the tracked LVTs crossed the reef, and the Japanese who had survived the bombardment returned to their firing pits. Half the LVTs were out of action by the end of the day. Marines were pinned against the log sea wall or stuck on the reef some 500 yards (460 m) offshore. Colonel Shoup, wounded soon after landing at the pier, took command ashore. By nightfall Sherman tanks had helped push the line about half-way across the island. Rear Admiral Shibazaki was killed in the afternoon by a shell that hit his headquarters party. By the end of the day 1,500 of the 5,000 Marines put ashore were casualties.

On 21 November Marines took Green Beach at the western end and crossed the airstrip. On 22 November the 6th Marines reached the eastern end of the airfield, and that night a Japanese assembly for a counterattack was broken up by artillery fire. At 03:00 on 23 November a banzai charge killed 45 Americans and wounded 128, and the Marines killed 325 attackers with destroyer support. Betio was declared secure at 13:30.
sections.aftermath:
The 2nd Battalion, 6th Marines cleared the other islands of the atoll by 28 November. Of the 3,636 Japanese in the garrison, only one officer and sixteen enlisted men survived. Of the 1,200 Korean labourers, 129 survived. In all 4,690 of the island's defenders were killed. The 2nd Marine Division lost 894 killed in action, 48 officers and 846 enlisted men, and a further 84 wounded died later. Another 2,188 men were wounded. Of the roughly 12,000 Marines of the division on Tarawa, 3,166 became casualties, nearly all in the 76 hours between the landing and the island being declared secure. Nearly 6,400 Japanese, Koreans and Americans died in the battle.

The losses caused public protest in the United States, which could not understand such heavy casualties for a small and seemingly unimportant island. General Holland Smith, who had toured the beaches, likened them to Pickett's Charge at Gettysburg, and Nimitz received angry letters from the families of the dead. The new Marine Corps Commandant, Alexander Vandegrift, told Congress that "Tarawa was an assault from beginning to end." A New York Times editorial of 27 December 1943 praised the Marines and warned that future assaults might cost more.

The 2nd Marine Division was shipped to Hawaii and was completely withdrawn by early 1944, leaving the 2nd Battalion, 6th Marines to clear the battlefield of ordnance, guard the Seabees rebuilding the airstrip and help with the burials. Nimitz launched the Marshalls campaign ten weeks after Tarawa, and aircraft flown from the airfields at Betio and Abemama proved highly valuable. The division fought its next major landing at Saipan in June 1944.
sections.sources:
The battle is known from the American side above all. War correspondent Robert Sherrod wrote a report for Time magazine, published on 6 December 1943, and Staff Sergeant Norman Hatch and other Marine cameramen filmed the beaches and the dead. Holland Smith's autobiography gives his later judgement on the operation. The Japanese command was largely cut off from its units once its communication lines were destroyed, and its commander was killed on the first day, so the Japanese conduct of the fighting is told mostly through the American record and the defences themselves.

The remains of the dead have added to the record. In November 2013 the remains of one American and four Japanese were recovered from a site that was considered pristine, with remains as they fell. The remains of 36 Marines, among them First Lieutenant Alexander Bonnyman Jr., lay in a battlefield cemetery whose location was lost by the end of the war and found in March 2015. In March 2019 a mass grave of Marines, reportedly of the 6th Marine Regiment, was found on Tarawa.

Several matters are open to question. Counts of the garrison differ, 4,500 defenders or 3,636, with about 5,000 men under arms including construction troops. The number of Japanese killed by the bombardment, put at least 40 per cent of the defenders, is an estimate, as is the toll of a single tank shot in the final advance, which destroyed the bodies so completely that it was put only at 50 to 75 men. Above all, whether the battle was worth its price is disputed, as the legacy shows.
sections.legacy:
Tarawa was the first time in the war that an American amphibious landing was opposed by well entrenched, determined defenders, and it was the most heavily defended atoll the Allies had invaded in the Pacific. Its significance for the Marshalls campaign lay in the lessons drawn. The casualties were put down to the miscalculation of the tide and the height of the reefs, the shortcomings of the landing craft, the inability of the naval bombardment to weaken a well entrenched enemy, and the difficulty of coordination between the services. Some three thousand shells were fired in the three hours before the landing, the heaviest bombardment of an invasion beach up to that time, but the high explosive shells usually went off before penetrating the defences. For the Marshalls the bombardments lasted a month and used armour-piercing shells, and the landing craft were armoured.

The failures at Tarawa were a major factor in founding the Underwater Demolition Teams, the precursor of the present US Navy SEALs. Rear Admiral Turner directed the formation of nine teams, and thirty officers and 150 enlisted men were moved to the Waimanalo Amphibious Training Base to form UDT One and UDT Two.

Judgement on the battle differed. Holland Smith wrote after the war that the decision to seize Tarawa was a mistake and the casualties needless. Nimitz, Spruance, Julian Smith and Shoup disagreed, and Nimitz said that the capture of Tarawa knocked down the front door to the Japanese defences in the Central Pacific. Sherrod wrote that Tarawa had been given a name to stand beside Concord Bridge, the Alamo and Belleau Wood. More than one hundred of the Americans killed were never repatriated, and the Marines recovered in 2015 and 2019 were returned to Hawaii.

summary: On 20 November 1943 the 2nd Marine Division landed on Betio in Tarawa Atoll and took it from its Japanese garrison in 76 hours. Nearly 6,400 Japanese, Koreans and Americans died, and the lessons of the landing shaped later operations in the Pacific.
references: Joseph H. Alexander, Utmost Savagery: The Three Days of Tarawa (Naval Institute Press, 1995)
Daniel Rogers, The Battle of Tarawa (Naval Institute Press, 2022)
John Wukovitz, One Square Mile of Hell: The Battle for Tarawa (NAL Trade, 2007)
Michael B Graham, Mantle of Heroism: Tarawa and the Struggle for the Gilberts, November 1943 (Presidio Press, 1998)
notes: Garrison size: the lead says 4,500 Japanese defenders, the infobox about 5,000 men under arms, the aftermath 3,636 Japanese plus 1,200 Korean laborers (4,690 killed). Both are given in the text; the article does not reconcile them.

Overlap: the 03:00 banzai charge (45 killed, 128 wounded, 325 Japanese killed) and the 04:00 attack on 1/6 (about 300 attackers, 200 dead in the lines and 125 beyond) are probably the same attack told twice; 1/6's losses are the same 45 and 128. I told it once, with the 03:00 figures.

The lead's sentence on the causes of heavy losses is informal ('many, very very short shelling period'); left out, the Lessons section is used instead. The lead also calls the victory 'decisive'; I did not repeat it.
Sherrod's '2,000 or 3,000 Marines, most of them now dead or wounded' is his own rough count and sits oddly with 3,166 casualties of 12,000; I note the two.

In the sources section the remark that the Japanese conduct is known mostly through the American record is my inference from the article's mention of destroyed communications; the article does not name Japanese sources. The editor may want to soften it.

Left out: the order of battle's lists of regiments, the Ryan's Orphans episode, the Bairiki landing and its twelve-gun pillbox that burned its own crew, details of individual tanks, Shoup's Medal of Honor citation, Frank Holland's later role.

Dates: the attack began at 09:00 and the landing is given as 09:10 in the aftermath; both are in the text. The article spells the Japanese admiral Shibazaki and in one infobox Shibasaki; I used Shibazaki. 'Tomonari Saichiro' is without macron.
The article writes 'U.S.' and 'meters'; I used British spelling and 'United States'. 'Fifty-fifty' kept as the article's 50–50.
